results.summary: This design implements a single-character UART transmitter using a 17-bit shift register built from D flip-flops and multiplexers. It transmits a user-selected ASCII character from 0x40 to 0x5F, including capital letters, at a 300 Hz clock rate. The design is tested by connecting an Arduino's serial RX pin to the output and configuring the Arduino serial monitor to 300 baud, then toggling switches to load and transmit the character. External hardware includes an Arduino and a computer with a serial monitor. The design is notable for its use of discrete flip-flops and multiplexers to implement the shift register, and it is a Wokwi-based project.

This design implements a UART transmitter capable of sending a string of multiple ASCII characters using five 21-bit shift registers. It operates at a 300 Hz clock and is controlled via switches for load, transmit, and output enable. Testing involves connecting an Arduino's serial RX pin to the output and setting the Arduino serial monitor to 300 baud, then toggling switches to transmit the string. External hardware includes an Arduino and a computer with a serial monitor. The design is notable for extending the single-character UART concept to strings and is implemented in Wokwi.

This design implements a customizable digital padlock that can be set to a user-defined code using switches. The code is entered via a push button, and the seven-segment display shows 'L' for locked and 'U' for unlocked. The design is tested by setting the code with switches, toggling the set switch, and then entering the code to unlock. No external hardware is required beyond the PCB's switches and display. The design is notable for being a simple embedded security application implemented in Wokwi.

This circuit outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display using a modulo-11 counter to sequence through characters. It operates at a 1 Hz clock and includes a reset input to restart the counter. Testing is done by simply powering the design and observing the display, with an optional reset toggle. No external hardware is required. The design is notable for its use of a counter and lookup logic to display a fixed message, and it is implemented in Wokwi.

This design simulates a 4-spin Ising chain in an external field using the Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo algorithm. It uses a 32-bit LFSR to generate random numbers for spin flip acceptance and can be chained with other instances to form longer chains. The design is tested by enabling neighbour inputs and observing the evolution to a ground state. No external hardware is required. The design is notable for being a self-contained physics simulation on a tiny tapeout chip, implemented in Wokwi.

This design implements a LUTRAM with a 4-bit address and 8-bit output, preloaded with a binary-to-7-segment decoder for digits 0-9. The memory content can be updated via clock and data pins, and a reset reverts to default data. Testing involves providing clock, data, reset, and address signals to display the corresponding digit. No external hardware is required. The design is notable for its use of a lookup table as memory and its limitation to 0-9 due to size constraints, implemented in Wokwi.

This design is a UART template that can be connected to an Arduino. It includes a clock and reset input and outputs to a 7-segment display. Testing is done by hooking it up to an Arduino. External hardware includes an Arduino. The documentation is very thin, providing only a title, one-line description, and minimal pin information, so the exact functionality is not fully described.

This design encodes binary-coded decimal (BCD) inputs in the range 0-9 to 7-segment display control signals. It was fully generated using a lookup table generator from a truth table, and invalid BCD inputs result in a blank display. Testing is done by setting the input switches and observing the displayed digit. External hardware includes input switches and a 7-segment display on the PCB. The design is notable for being automatically generated from a truth table, implemented in Wokwi.

This design implements a state machine to control German traffic lights at an intersection with main and side streets, including pedestrian signals. It operates at a 1 Hz clock and generates a blinking yellow light for the side street in the reset state. Testing requires providing a clock, connecting LEDs, and generating a reset signal; an additional inverter is needed for pedestrian red signals. External hardware includes LEDs and an inverter. The design is notable for modeling a specific traffic light sequence, implemented in Wokwi.

This design reads inputs from external photodiodes, sums the binary values, and displays the total on a 7-segment display. It includes a clock and reset input, and can be tested using dip switches instead of photodiodes, with a switch to select step or continuous sampling mode. External hardware includes a breadboard, resistors, and photodiodes. The design is notable for interfacing with analog sensors to display light intensity, implemented in Wokwi.
